Golden ratio.long:
The golden ratio is roughly 1.618, a number that appears when each term of the Fibonacci sequence is divided by the one before it. Trading material treats it, and its inverse 0.618, as naturally significant levels for retracements and extensions.

The mathematics is real; the market claim built on it is not. No documented mechanism connects a ratio found in sunflower heads to the depth of a pullback in a futures contract. Prices are set by orders, and orders cluster at levels people watch — which is the one honest sense in which the ratio can matter: enough traders drawing the same tool at the same swing points creates a modest self-fulfilling focal point.

Even that weaker claim is hard to test, because the choice of which swing to anchor from is discretionary, and different anchors put the 61.8 level in different places.

Where people get fooled: pullbacks of many depths happen constantly, so some inevitably stop near a golden-ratio level. Counting those hits while ignoring the misses, and re-anchoring until the tool fits, produces the illusion of precision from what is actually a wide net.
Golden ratio.usage: Generally cited as the basis for the 61.8 retracement and 1.618 extension levels; sceptics note the anchoring freedom does most of the work.

Fibonacci extension.long:
A Fibonacci extension projects a target beyond the end of a move, by taking the length of a prior swing and multiplying it by ratios such as 1.272 or 1.618, then measuring that distance from a chosen anchor point.

The mechanism on offer is the same as for retracements: either the ratios matter intrinsically, for which there is no documented cause, or enough traders project the same targets that resting orders gather there. The second is plausible in heavily watched markets but modest in size, and it competes with every other reason a level might matter — prior highs, round numbers, option strikes.

What extensions genuinely provide is a pre-committed target. Deciding before entry where the trade will be closed is valuable discipline regardless of how the level was generated, because it removes the mid-trade negotiation with yourself.

Where people get fooled: three anchor choices — swing start, swing end, retracement point — each with discretion, generate a spread of possible targets wide enough that one of them is nearly always hit. The tool then takes credit for an outcome the spread guaranteed.
Fibonacci extension.usage: Typically used to set profit targets beyond a breakout or impulse move; the discipline of a pre-set target is the defensible part.

Equilibrium / 50% level.long:
The equilibrium or 50 percent level is the midpoint of a prior swing — halfway between its high and low. Modern structure-based material treats price above the midpoint as premium and below it as discount, and prefers buying in discount and selling in premium.

The midpoint is not a Fibonacci number, and its appeal is simpler: it is the one level on the retracement tool that needs no theory. A pullback that holds half of the prior move has kept most of its conviction; one that gives it all back has not. Framed that way, the 50 level is a rough measure of how one-sided the swing remains, which is an observation about the auction rather than a prediction.

Dividing the range into halves also gives a consistent language for where in a move an entry is taken, which helps a journal say something comparable across trades.

Where people get fooled: treating the midpoint as a wall. It is a reference, not a mechanism — nothing rests there except whatever orders happen to rest there, and half of all pullbacks must end either side of it by construction.
Equilibrium / 50% level.usage: Generally used as a reference for whether price sits in the upper or lower half of a prior swing, often alongside premium and discount language.

Elliott Wave.long:
Elliott Wave theory, from Ralph Nelson Elliott's work in the 1930s, holds that markets move in a repeating structure: five waves in the trend direction, three against it, with the pattern nesting inside itself at every scale.

The idea is genuinely elegant, and Elliott catalogued it with care. The difficulty is that the framework has never produced testable predictions that survive scrutiny, because its rules permit revision: a count that fails becomes a different count, waves extend, corrections turn complex, and the labelling moves to accommodate whatever happened. A theory that can absorb any outcome cannot be falsified, and a framework that cannot be falsified cannot be validated either.

Practitioners answer that counting is a skill, and poor counts are the counter's fault. That defence is unfalsifiable in the same way, since skill is only ever demonstrated after the fact.

Where people get fooled: the retrospective charts are immaculate — every historical move labels beautifully once it is over. The live experience is several competing counts at once, each implying a different trade, with the surviving count chosen by hindsight and presented as if it had been the forecast.
Elliott Wave.usage: Generally used as a narrative framework for where a move sits within a larger cycle; its counts are contested territory rather than settled readings.

Wave count.long:
A wave count is the labelling of a chart according to Elliott's structure — numbering the impulse waves one to five and lettering the corrective waves A, B, C, at whatever degree of trend is being analysed.

The rules are specific enough to sound rigorous: wave two cannot retrace all of wave one, wave three is never the shortest, wave four should not overlap wave one. In practice these constraints still leave multiple legal counts on most charts, and analysts maintain a preferred count plus alternates. When price violates the preferred count, an alternate is promoted, and the framework continues without ever having been wrong in its own terms.

The count does force close attention to swing structure, proportion and momentum, and some traders value it for that discipline alone — the labels make you look carefully, even if the labels themselves carry no authority.

Where people get fooled: the alternate-count mechanism means the method never fails, it only re-labels. A tool that cannot fail teaches nothing, and confidence built on it compounds precisely because no losing count is ever recorded as the method's loss.
Wave count.usage: Typically maintained as a preferred count with alternates in Elliott-based analysis; the revision habit is what critics point at.

Impulse vs corrective.long:
In wave terminology an impulse is a strong directional move, said to run in five sub-waves with the trend, while a corrective move is the slower, overlapping structure that retraces part of it, typically in three sub-waves.

Stripped of the counting apparatus, the underlying observation is sound and much older than Elliott: markets alternate between directional legs and congestion, and the directional legs tend to be faster, cleaner and less overlapped than the pauses between them. Reading whether current price action is impulsive or corrective — is this move being driven, or is it drifting — is a genuinely useful lens, because it describes the present rather than predicting the future.

Trend traders use the distinction without any wave vocabulary: enter with the impulses, tolerate the corrections, leave when the impulses stop coming.

Where people get fooled: the classification is obvious after a leg completes and ambiguous during it. Every correction begins with a bar that looks impulsive against the trend, and every failed trend resumes one last time before rolling over. Naming the two states is easy; separating them live is the entire difficulty, and the names do none of that work.
Impulse vs corrective.usage: Generally used to describe whether current price action is driving or drifting; useful as description even outside wave analysis.

ABCD pattern.long:
The ABCD is a four-point pattern: a move from A to B, a retracement to C, then a second move to D that mirrors the first leg in length and often in time. Traders watch for the completion at D as a place where the swing may exhaust.

The honest core is symmetry. Markets do show a tendency for measured legs — a second push of similar size to the first — because the participants who drove the first leg often have similar size and similar targets on the second. The measured-move idea in classical charting is the same observation, decades older than the harmonic vocabulary that now surrounds it.

As with all projection tools, its practical value is mostly the pre-commitment: D is defined before price arrives, so the trader has a plan rather than a reaction.

Where people get fooled: tolerance. If D counts as reached anywhere within a generous band, and the pattern can be redrawn from other swing points when the first attempt misses, the hit rate observed is a property of the flexibility, not the market. Fix the anchors and the tolerance before judging it, and count the misses.
ABCD pattern.usage: Typically used to project where a second swing leg matches the first; the older name for the idea is a measured move.

Harmonic patterns.long:
Harmonic patterns are multi-leg formations — Gartley, Bat, Butterfly, Crab and relatives — defined by specific Fibonacci relationships between successive swings. Each has a completion zone where the ratios converge and a reversal is anticipated.

The framework descends from H.M. Gartley's 1935 book, with the ratio specifications added by later authors. Its distinguishing feature is precision: each pattern demands particular retracement and extension values, which gives it the appearance of engineering. But precision in the definition is not evidence in the market — it just means the pattern is rarer, not more predictive, and the tolerance bands applied in practice hand back most of the precision anyway.

No independent validation of harmonic completion zones exists at standards a statistician would accept, and the anchoring and tolerance freedoms make private backtests of them fragile.

Where people get fooled: the specificity is persuasive in itself — a pattern with five measured legs and named ratios feels like it must encode something. Complexity is doing the persuading, not evidence. A rule with more parameters fits history more easily and predicts the future less well, and harmonics carry a lot of parameters.
Harmonic patterns.usage: Generally traded as reversal setups at ratio-defined completion zones; treat any claimed reliability as unsourced until shown otherwise.

Gartley.long:
The Gartley is the original harmonic pattern, named for H.M. Gartley, who sketched the shape in his 1935 book Profits in the Stock Market. The modern version is a five-point structure — X, A, B, C, D — where the D point completes near the 78.6 retracement of the initial XA leg, with internal legs meeting their own ratio requirements.

Gartley's own book, worth noting, did not contain the precise Fibonacci specifications now attached to his name; those were added by later authors, notably in the 1990s. The pattern as traded today is therefore a modern construction wearing a 1935 citation, which matters when its age is offered as evidence of durability.

Mechanically, the pattern describes a retracement that fails to make a new extreme — a lower high in an uptrend's pullback structure — which is an ordinary and reasonable thing to watch.

Where people get fooled: the pedigree. Old name, precise ratios and a completion zone create an impression of tested machinery, but the specification changed hands and tightened long after the citation date, and no version of it has published validation. Judge it as you would any untested rule: by logging your own attempts, misses included.
Gartley.usage: Typically traded as a retracement-failure reversal at a ratio-defined D point; the modern ratio rules postdate the 1935 source they cite.

Gann.long:
W.D. Gann was an early twentieth-century trader whose methods — Gann angles, squares, and time-price relationships — treat time and price as geometrically linked, with trend strength read from the angle of advance and turning points projected from past ranges.

Gann's material is voluminous, obscure, and often deliberately cryptic; his followers disagree about what the method even is, which makes evaluation difficult before evidence enters the picture. The angles themselves have a technical flaw a modern reader spots immediately: a 45-degree line depends entirely on the chart's scale, so the same market drawn on two different price axes produces different Gann angles. A signal that changes with the axis is a property of the drawing, not the market.

Claims about Gann's personal fortune, often used to sell the method, are unverified and disputed; contemporary accounts differ sharply from the marketing version.

Where people get fooled: obscurity working as authority. Material this dense invites the assumption that difficulty conceals depth, and every failed application can be attributed to misunderstanding the master. A method whose failures always indict the student and never the method has removed itself from testing.
Gann.usage: Generally encountered through Gann angles and square-of-nine tools; the scale-dependence of the angles is the standard technical objection.

Time cycles.long:
Time-cycle analysis holds that markets turn at rhythmic intervals — fixed periods, anniversaries of prior highs and lows, or harmonics of longer cycles — so that when a move happens matters as much as where price sits.

Some periodicity in markets is real and documented: seasonal patterns in commodities tied to harvests and heating demand, options expiry effects on particular days, and the business cycle at the scale of years. These have mechanisms — physical supply, contractual dates, credit conditions. The cycle analysis sold to traders usually claims far more: precise turn dates projected from chart geometry, with no mechanism on offer.

Detecting genuine cycles in noisy data is a hard statistical problem, and spectral methods applied to price series mostly find cycles that shift, fade and reappear — consistent with noise being read as rhythm.

Where people get fooled: a projected turn date needs only a generous window to seem vindicated, because markets turn somewhere every few days. Hit within three days either side, claim the cycle; miss, and the cycle inverted or a longer cycle dominated. With those outs available, the record of any turn-date method is unfalsifiable by design.
Time cycles.usage: Typically encountered as projected turn dates or anniversary counts; documented calendar effects with mechanisms are the narrow honest core.
